lessons.title: Reactivity of metals
lessons.summary: Discover how metals react with oxygen, water and acids, build the reactivity series, and use it to predict displacement reactions and explain how metals are extracted.
objectives: I can describe oxidation and reduction in terms of oxygen gain and loss.
I can place metals in order of reactivity using their reactions with water and dilute acids.
I can predict displacement reactions using the reactivity series.
I can explain how a metal's position in the reactivity series affects how it is extracted.
I can identify oxidation and reduction in terms of electron transfer (Higher).

activities.title: Metals and oxygen
activities.content:
## Oxidation and reduction

Most metals react with oxygen in the air to form a **metal oxide**. A shiny piece of magnesium ribbon burns with a brilliant white flame:

2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO

When a substance **gains oxygen** it has been **oxidised**. When a substance **loses oxygen** it has been **reduced**.

These two always happen together. If one substance gains oxygen, something else must have lost it. For example, when iron oxide is heated with carbon:

2Fe₂O₃ + 3C → 4Fe + 3CO₂

- Iron oxide **loses** oxygen, so it is **reduced**.
- Carbon **gains** oxygen, so it is **oxidised**.

A reaction where one thing is reduced and another oxidised is called a **redox** reaction.

Rusting is a slow oxidation of iron. Gold does not react with oxygen at all, which is one reason it stays shiny for thousands of years. That difference between magnesium, iron and gold is what we mean by **reactivity**.

activities.title: Worked example: spotting oxidation and reduction
activities.content:
**Copper oxide is heated with hydrogen: CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O. Which substance is oxidised and which is reduced?**

Look at where the oxygen goes.

| Substance | Before | After | Oxygen | So it is... |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| CuO | has oxygen | Cu, no oxygen | lost | **reduced** |
| H₂ | no oxygen | H₂O, has oxygen | gained | **oxidised** |

Copper oxide is reduced to copper. Hydrogen is oxidised to water.

**Tip:** ask "who has oxygen at the start, and who has it at the end?" The oxygen has moved from the copper to the hydrogen.

question.text: In the reaction ZnO + C → Zn + CO, which statement is correct?
question.hint: Follow the oxygen. Which substance has it at the start, and which has it at the end?
question.explanation: Zinc oxide loses its oxygen, so it is reduced. Carbon gains oxygen to become carbon monoxide, so it is oxidised.

options.text: Zinc oxide is reduced and carbon is oxidised.
Zinc oxide is oxidised and carbon is reduced.
options.feedback: Zinc oxide loses oxygen, and losing oxygen is reduction.
Oxidation and reduction always happen together in a redox reaction.
Carbon gains oxygen, which is oxidation.

activities.title: Reactions with water and acids
activities.content:
## Building the reactivity series

We can rank metals by how vigorously they react.

### With water

**Metal + water → metal hydroxide + hydrogen**

- **Potassium** fizzes violently, melts into a ball and often ignites with a lilac flame.
- **Sodium** fizzes rapidly and melts into a ball.
- **Lithium** and **calcium** fizz steadily.
- **Magnesium** barely reacts with cold water, but reacts with steam.
- **Zinc, iron, copper** show no visible reaction with cold water.

### With dilute acid

**Metal + acid → salt + hydrogen**

This test separates the middle metals. Magnesium fizzes fast, zinc fizzes steadily, iron fizzes slowly, and copper does nothing at all.

### The reactivity series

From most to least reactive:

**potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, (carbon), zinc, iron, (hydrogen), copper, silver, gold**

Carbon and hydrogen are not metals, but they are included because they help us predict extraction and acid reactions.

### Why are some metals more reactive?

When a metal reacts it **loses electrons** to form a **positive ion**. The more easily a metal gives up its electrons, the more reactive it is. Potassium loses its outer electron very easily; gold holds on to its electrons tightly.

activities.title: Worked example: reading the observations
activities.content:
**A student adds three unknown metals, A, B and C, to dilute hydrochloric acid and to cold water.**

| Metal | Cold water | Dilute acid |
|---|---|---|
| A | no change | slow bubbling |
| B | rapid fizzing, metal melts | (too dangerous to test) |
| C | no change | fast fizzing |

**Put A, B and C in order of reactivity.**

- B reacts strongly with cold water, so it is the most reactive. It is probably a group 1 metal such as sodium.
- C does not react with water but fizzes fast with acid, so it is in the middle, like magnesium.
- A reacts only slowly with acid, so it is the least reactive of the three, like iron.

Order: **B > C > A**

Notice that the rate of bubbling in acid is what lets us separate A from C. Water alone would not have told us.

question.text: Arrange these metals in order of reactivity, starting with the MOST reactive.
question.hint: Group 1 metals are at the top; copper and gold are near the bottom.
question.explanation: Sodium is a group 1 metal and the most reactive here. Then calcium, magnesium, zinc, iron and finally copper, which does not even react with dilute acid.

metadata.blanksText:
metal + water → metal ___ + hydrogen

metal + acid → ___ + hydrogen

When a metal reacts it forms a positive ion by ___ electrons.

question.hint: Metals with water make an alkaline compound. Metals with acid make a salt. Metal atoms give away electrons.
question.explanation: Metals react with water to give a metal hydroxide and hydrogen; with acids to give a salt and hydrogen; and they form positive ions by losing electrons.

activities.title: Displacement reactions
activities.content:
## A more reactive metal pushes out a less reactive one

If you drop a strip of zinc into blue copper sulfate solution, the zinc slowly turns brown as copper metal coats it, and the blue colour fades:

Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu

Zinc is **more reactive** than copper, so it takes the sulfate for itself and **displaces** the copper. The reverse does not happen: copper cannot displace zinc from zinc sulfate.

**Rule:** a metal will displace a less reactive metal from a compound (in solution or as a solid).

### Electron transfer (Higher tier)

In the zinc and copper sulfate reaction the sulfate ions are not involved at all. They are **spectator ions**. The ionic equation shows only what changes:

Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu

- Zinc atoms **lose** two electrons: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻. Loss of electrons is **oxidation**.
- Copper ions **gain** two electrons: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu. Gain of electrons is **reduction**.

The memory aid **OIL RIG** helps: **O**xidation **I**s **L**oss, **R**eduction **I**s **G**ain (of electrons).

This electron definition works for every redox reaction, even ones with no oxygen in them at all.

activities.title: Worked example: predicting displacement
activities.content:
**Will a reaction happen in each case?**

**1. Magnesium added to iron(II) sulfate solution**

Magnesium is above iron in the series, so **yes**:

Mg + FeSO₄ → MgSO₄ + Fe

You would see grey iron forming on the magnesium and the pale green colour of the solution fading.

**2. Silver added to copper nitrate solution**

Silver is below copper, so **no reaction**. The silver simply sits there.

**3. Iron added to copper chloride solution (Higher: write the ionic equation)**

Iron is above copper, so yes:

Fe + Cu²⁺ → Fe²⁺ + Cu

Iron is oxidised (loses electrons); copper ions are reduced (gain electrons). The chloride ions are spectators and are left out.

question.text: Which of the following mixtures would produce a displacement reaction? Select all that apply.
question.hint: A reaction happens only when the added metal is higher in the reactivity series than the metal in the compound.
question.explanation: Zinc is above iron, and magnesium is above copper, so those two react. Copper is below magnesium and silver is below zinc, so no reaction happens in those cases.

options.feedback: Copper is less reactive than magnesium, so it cannot displace it.
Silver is near the bottom of the series and cannot displace zinc.

activities.title: Extracting metals from their ores
activities.content:
## Where the reactivity series really matters

A few unreactive metals, such as **gold**, are found in the ground as the pure metal. Most metals are found as compounds, usually oxides, in rocks called **ores**. To get the metal out, the oxide must be **reduced**.

### Metals below carbon

Metals **less reactive than carbon** (zinc, iron, copper, and so on) can be extracted by heating the oxide with carbon. Carbon is more reactive, so it takes the oxygen:

2ZnO + C → 2Zn + CO₂

The metal oxide is reduced; the carbon is oxidised. This is cheap because carbon (as coke) is plentiful.

### Metals above carbon

Metals **more reactive than carbon** (aluminium, magnesium, sodium and so on) cannot be reduced by carbon. They are extracted by **electrolysis** of the molten compound, which needs a lot of electrical energy and so is expensive. You will meet this in the electrolysis lesson.

### Summary table

| Position | Example | Method |
|---|---|---|
| Above carbon | Al, Mg, Na | electrolysis |
| Below carbon | Zn, Fe, Cu | reduction with carbon |
| Very unreactive | Au | found native (uncombined) |

question.text: Match each metal to the way it is usually obtained.
question.hint: Compare each metal's position with carbon in the reactivity series.
question.explanation: Aluminium is above carbon so needs electrolysis. Iron is below carbon so its oxide can be reduced with carbon. Gold is so unreactive it occurs uncombined in the ground.

pairs.right: found in the ground as the pure metal

question.text:
A student places a piece of magnesium ribbon in a test tube of blue copper(II) sulfate solution.

(a) Describe two things the student would observe.

(b) Explain, in terms of reactivity, why this reaction happens.

(c) **Higher tier:** Write the ionic equation for the reaction and state which species is oxidised.
question.hint: Think about the colour of the solution, what forms on the magnesium, and which metal is higher in the reactivity series.
question.explanation: (a) The blue solution fades or goes colourless, and a brown/pink solid (copper) forms on the magnesium; the magnesium gets smaller and the tube warms up. (b) Magnesium is more reactive than copper, so it displaces copper from the solution. (c) Mg + Cu²⁺ → Mg²⁺ + Cu. Magnesium is oxidised because it loses electrons.

markScheme.criterion: Blue colour of the solution fades / becomes colourless
Brown or pink solid (copper) forms on the magnesium (or magnesium disappears / temperature rises)
Magnesium is more reactive than copper, so it displaces copper
Ionic equation Mg + Cu²⁺ → Mg²⁺ + Cu and magnesium is oxidised (loses electrons)

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- **Oxidation** = gain of oxygen (or loss of electrons). **Reduction** = loss of oxygen (or gain of electrons). OIL RIG.
- Reactivity is judged by reactions with **water** and **dilute acid**: metal + water → hydroxide + H₂; metal + acid → salt + H₂.
- The reactivity series (high to low): K, Na, Li, Ca, Mg, Al, **C**, Zn, Fe, **H**, Cu, Ag, Au.
- A more reactive metal **displaces** a less reactive one from its compound.
- Metals below carbon are extracted by **reduction with carbon**; metals above carbon need **electrolysis**; gold is found native.
- Reactivity depends on how easily the metal atom **loses electrons** to form a positive ion.

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: when a metal reacts with dilute acid, the gas produced is hydrogen.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think of the general equation metal + acid → ?
practiceQuestions.explanation: True. Metal + acid → salt + hydrogen. The hydrogen gives a squeaky pop with a lit splint.

practiceQuestions.text: Which metal reacts most violently with cold water?
practiceQuestions.hint: Group 1 metals are the most reactive metals.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Potassium is at the top of the reactivity series and reacts violently with cold water, often igniting with a lilac flame.

options.feedback: Magnesium reacts only very slowly with cold water.

practiceQuestions.text: Complete the sentence about redox reactions.

metadata.blanksText: In the reaction 2CuO + C → 2Cu + CO₂, copper oxide is ___ because it loses oxygen, and carbon is ___ because it gains oxygen.

practiceQuestions.hint: Gaining oxygen and losing oxygen have opposite names.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Loss of oxygen is reduction; gain of oxygen is oxidation.

practiceQuestions.text: Why can iron be extracted from iron oxide by heating with carbon, but aluminium cannot be extracted from aluminium oxide the same way?
practiceQuestions.hint: Compare each metal with carbon in the reactivity series.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Carbon can only remove oxygen from a metal that is less reactive than itself. Iron is below carbon; aluminium is above it.

options.text: Iron is less reactive than carbon, but aluminium is more reactive than carbon.
Iron oxide contains more oxygen than aluminium oxide.
Aluminium oxide is a liquid at room temperature.
Carbon reacts with aluminium to form an alloy.

practiceQuestions.text: A student adds copper to a solution of silver nitrate. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
practiceQuestions.hint: Copper is above silver in the reactivity series.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Copper is more reactive than silver, so it displaces silver: grey silver crystals form and the solution turns blue as copper ions form. Copper atoms lose electrons, so copper is oxidised.

options.feedback: Silver ions gain electrons, so they are reduced.

options.text: No reaction happens because copper is unreactive.
options.feedback: Copper is low in the series, but still above silver.

practiceQuestions.text: Order these metals from LEAST reactive to MOST reactive.
practiceQuestions.hint: Gold is the least reactive metal in the series.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Gold < copper < iron < zinc < aluminium < calcium.

practiceQuestions.text: Iron is extracted from iron(III) oxide: 2Fe₂O₃ + 3C → 4Fe + 3CO₂. Calculate the mass of iron, in grams, produced from 32 g of iron(III) oxide. (Mr of Fe₂O₃ = 160, Ar of Fe = 56)
practiceQuestions.hint: Find moles of Fe₂O₃, then use the 2 : 4 ratio, then multiply by 56.
practiceQuestions.explanation: moles Fe₂O₃ = 32 ÷ 160 = 0.2 mol. Ratio 2 : 4 gives 0.4 mol Fe. mass = 0.4 × 56 = 22.4 g.

practiceQuestions.text: Higher tier: match each half-equation to its description.
practiceQuestions.hint: OIL RIG: oxidation is loss of electrons, reduction is gain.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ loses electrons (oxidation). Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu gains electrons (reduction). SO₄²⁻ does not change, so it is a spectator ion.

practiceQuestions.text: A student wants to compare the reactivity of magnesium, zinc and iron. Describe a method the student could use, and state what they should observe to decide the order.
practiceQuestions.hint: Use dilute acid, keep everything the same except the metal, and compare the fizzing.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Add equal-sized pieces of each metal to the same volume and concentration of dilute hydrochloric acid at the same temperature. Compare how fast bubbles of hydrogen are produced (or measure temperature rise). The fastest fizzing is the most reactive, so magnesium > zinc > iron.

markScheme.criterion: Add each metal to dilute acid (e.g. hydrochloric acid)
Keep the acid volume/concentration, temperature and metal size the same (fair test)
Compare the rate of bubbling / fizzing (or temperature change); fastest is the most reactive

practiceQuestions.text:
Metal X is found in the ground as its oxide. When the oxide is heated strongly with carbon, metal X is produced. Metal X does not react with cold water but reacts slowly with dilute acid to give bubbles.

(a) Suggest which metal X could be. Give a reason.

(b) Name the type of reaction in which the oxide is converted to the metal, and explain what happens to the oxygen.

(c) Explain why sodium cannot be extracted from sodium oxide using carbon.
practiceQuestions.hint: Which metals are below carbon, do not react with cold water, but do react slowly with acid?
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) Iron (or zinc): it is below carbon, does not react with cold water, and reacts slowly with acid. (b) Reduction: the metal oxide loses oxygen to the carbon, which is oxidised. (c) Sodium is more reactive than carbon, so carbon cannot take the oxygen from it; electrolysis is needed instead.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies X as iron (or zinc) with a reason linked to its position in the reactivity series
The oxide loses oxygen (to the carbon, which is oxidised)
Sodium is more reactive than carbon, so carbon cannot displace/reduce it
